results.content: # An Expert Guide to Forecast Error Variance Decomposition. Master FEVD basics and tools for confident forecasts. Explore the fundamentals of forecast error variance decomposition, from theoretical foundations in VAR models to practical Python examples and best practices. Forecast Error Variance Decomposition (FEVD) is a technique used in multivariate time series analysis to apportion the variance of the forecast error for each variable to shocks in all variables in the system. * Helps policymakers and analysts understand which shocks drive variability at different horizons. ### 2.1 Vector Autoregression (VAR) Models. A VAR(p) model for an *n*-dimensional time series yt​ is defined as:. • εt​ is an i.i.d. error term with covariance matrix Σ (Lütkepohl, 2005). The FEVD for variable *i* at horizon *h* due to shock in variable *j* is:. The denominator is the total forecast error variance of variable *i* up to horizon *h*. 1. **Estimate the VAR model**. • Fit VAR(p) to your multivariate series. • Select lag length via AIC/BIC. 3. **Derive forecast error variance**. • Total variance for variable *i* at horizon *h*:. 4. **Allocate variance to shocks**. • Compute θij​(h) for each pair *(i, j)*. * **Model misspecification**: Incorrect lag choice or omitted variables bias FEVD. Fit VAR model model = VAR(data_diff) results = model.fit(maxlags=8, ic='aic') print(results.summary()) # 3. Compute FEVD fevd = results.fevd(10) # horizons 1..10 # 4. Display & plot for i, col in enumerate(data_diff.columns): df = fevd.decomp[:, i, :] * 100 # percentage contributions df.plot(title=f'FEVD for {col}', xlabel='Horizon', ylabel='Percent'). * Computes FEVD up to 10 steps. • **Ensure stationarity**: Use unit‐root tests (ADF, KPSS) and difference or detrend as needed. • **Multicollinearity**: Highly correlated variables can distort coefficient estimates; consider PCA or dropping redundant series. * FEVD quantifies the share of forecast error variance attributable to each shock. Whether you are a researcher, policy‐maker, or data‐science practitioner, mastering FEVD will deepen your understanding of multivariate dynamics and improve the interpretability of your forecasting models. results.title: Forecast Error Variance Decomposition Guide
results.content: Forecast Error Variance Decomposition (FEVD) is a crucial tool in the realm of multivariate time series analysis. It provides insight into how different types of shocks contribute to the forecast error variance of each variable in a system. FEVD measures the proportion of the variance of the forecast error for each variable that can be attributed to innovations (or shocks) within the system at different forecast horizons. In time series analysis, especially when using vector autoregressive (VAR) models, FEVD is used to:. While Impulse Response Functions (IRFs) trace the effect of a one-time shock on the variables within the system over time, FEVD takes a complementary perspective by:. * **Quantifying the Effects**: Instead of just showing the impulse response, FEVD decomposes the forecast error variance into contributions from each shock. flowchart TD A["VAR Model"] --> B["Impulse Response Functions"] A --> C["Forecast Error Variance Decomposition"] B --> D["Time Path of Shock Effects"] C --> E["Contribution Percentages"]. To understand FEVD, one must delve into its theoretical underpinnings, primarily rooted in VAR models and the associated methods for disentangling shocks. This decomposition is fundamental when computing FEVD because it isolates the impact of independent shocks on each variable. Cholesky decomposition is a key step to orthogonalize the shocks for FEVD computation. flowchart TD A["Prepare Data"] B["Estimate VAR Model"] C["Compute Residuals and Covariance"] D["Cholesky Decomposition"] E["Obtain Orthogonal Shocks"] F["Calculate Moving Average Representation"] G["Compute FEVD"] A --> B B --> C C --> D D --> E E --> F F --> G. FEVD outputs typically give a percentage breakdown of how much each shock contributes to the forecast error variance for a specific variable. Forecast Error Variance Decomposition is a cornerstone technique in modern time series analysis, particularly in the use of VAR models. Whether you are an economist deciphering the contributions of monetary and fiscal shocks or a financial analyst managing portfolio risks, FEVD is an invaluable tool for enhancing forecast accuracy and deepening model interpretation. As time series analysis continues to evolve with growing data availability and computational power, tools like FEVD will remain central to unlocking the complexities of dynamic systems, guiding both strategic planning and policy formulation.
